text: You are twelve years old.
The air smells of dust, and sweat, and leather.
In front of you, a black horse is screaming and rearing, higher than the men around him.
They call him Bucephalus.
Your father's best riders have tried him, one after another. And every one has been thrown, or has backed away.
Your father is tired of it. He tells them to take the horse away.
And the men nod, because that's what you do, when the king has decided.
But you've been watching. Not the horse's hooves. His eyes.
Every time he lunges, he's jumping away from something on the ground.
His own shadow. Black, and moving at his feet.
The men are laughing at you for speaking up. Your father is watching, to see if you'll embarrass him.
Your heart is pounding.
What do you do?
You walk forward, slowly.
You take the reins, and turn his head toward the sun, so the shadow falls behind him, where he can't see it.
You speak low. You put your hand on his neck, and feel him trembling under your palm.
Then, in one motion, you're on his back.
And you let him run.
When you ride back, your father has tears in his eyes.
My son, he says. Find a kingdom big enough for you. Macedonia is too small.
Feel what just happened inside you. Not the applause. Something quieter.
A part of you watched you see what the grown men missed. And it wrote it down.
I see what others miss. I move when others give up.
That's the Observer. It doesn't believe what you say about yourself. It believes what it sees you do.
You've had moments like this. Fixing what the adults gave up on. Finishing the rep, when everyone else racked the weight.
Nobody throws a party. But a belief is born.
What's the last thing you did, that gave your Observer real evidence?
